**On Folding**

There is a moment, when you fold a sheet of paper in half, where the paper resists. Not much. A slight springiness under the thumb, a wish to return to flatness. Then the crease sets, and the paper has a memory it did not have before. It will never again lie entirely flat. You have given it a history.

I think about this more than I probably should. Folding is one of the oldest things we do that isn't strictly necessary for survival, and yet we do it constantly, almost without noticing. We fold laundry, letters, maps, napkins, dough, our arms, our hands, our legs beneath us on a couch. We fold ideas into other ideas. We fold time, in a sense, every time we remember: the past is brought up against the present, edge to edge, and pressed.

Consider the map. A road map, the paper kind, the kind that lived in the glove compartment of every car for most of a century. The genius of it was not the cartography but the folding. A sheet three feet wide collapsed into something the size of a paperback, and then—this is the part that mattered—it could be opened partway. You could unfold just the panel you needed, the one with your county on it, and leave the rest of the state tucked away. The map was designed to be read in pieces. Its folds were a kind of index.

Of course, no one could ever refold one correctly. This was a universal human failing, a comedy that crossed cultures. You'd try, and the creases would fight you, insisting on a sequence you couldn't reconstruct, and you'd end up with a lumpy, bulging thing that no longer fit where it came from. The map remembered its proper shape better than you did. There is something humbling in being outwitted by paper.

Letters, too, were folded, and for a long time the fold was the envelope. Before mass-produced envelopes, you wrote on one side of a sheet, folded it in a particular way so that the writing was inside, sealed it with wax, and addressed the outside. The letter was its own container. Historians who study these things—"letterlocking," they call it—have found that people developed elaborate, personal folding patterns, some with little tucks and slits that would tear if anyone opened the letter before the intended reader. The fold was privacy. The fold was a lock. When you unfolded a letter from a friend, you were also undoing a small act of care, a bit of deliberate geometry made just for you.

I find that lovely, and a little sad, because almost none of us fold anything for anyone anymore. Our messages arrive unfolded, already open, flat on a glass screen. Nothing resists the thumb.

Mountains are folds. This is not a metaphor. When two plates of the earth's crust push against each other, the rock between them buckles, and the buckling is what we call the Alps, the Himalayas, the Appalachians. If you look at a road cut through certain hillsides you can see it plainly: layers of stone that were once flat as a lakebed now bent into arches and troughs, the way a rug wrinkles when you shove a couch across it. The earth has been folding for four billion years and shows no sign of getting the sequence right either. It just keeps pressing, and the creases keep setting, and we build ski resorts on the results.

And then there are proteins, which are the folds that make us. A protein begins as a chain—a long string of amino acids, essentially a sentence written in a twenty-letter alphabet. The sentence itself does nothing. It is only when the chain folds, curling and tucking into a precise three-dimensional shape, that it becomes a thing that can act: an enzyme, a receptor, a strand of hair. The folding happens in microseconds and it happens correctly almost every time, which is astonishing, because the number of possible ways a chain could fold is so vast that if it tried them randomly it would take longer than the age of the universe. Somehow the chain knows. Or rather, the chain doesn't know anything; the folding is simply what happens when that particular sentence meets water and warmth. The shape is already implied in the sequence. The fold is the meaning of the string.

When proteins fold wrong, we get diseases—Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, cystic fibrosis. Misfolded proteins clump together, forget their jobs, gum up the works. Life, it turns out, depends on getting the creases right, and the map does not come with instructions.

So perhaps it's not surprising that folding feels meaningful to us at a level below thought. When someone folds your laundry, it registers as intimacy. When a child hands you a paper crane, you keep it, even though it's just paper, because it contains a sequence of decisions—this corner here, this edge to that one—and the decisions were made for you. A folded thing is a thing that has been handled. It carries the print of attention.

I once watched an old woman fold a fitted sheet, which is the one domestic feat I have never mastered. She did it in the air, without a table, tucking the elastic corners into each other in a way that seemed to violate topology, and in about eight seconds she had a neat rectangle. I asked her how. She said she didn't know; her hands knew. She had been folding that shape for sixty years, and the sequence had gone into her body the way a crease goes into paper.

That is the last thing I want to say about folding: that it goes both ways. We fold the paper and the paper folds us. Every repeated gesture leaves a line. We are all, by middle age, a lumpy map of the things we have done over and over—the tilt of the head when we listen, the way we hold a cup, the particular slump we settle into when we're tired. We could not refold ourselves into flatness if we tried. And I'm not sure we'd want to. A flat sheet has no history. It has never been held. Give me the creased thing, the one that springs a little under the thumb, the one that remembers.
